The ministers of the cult publicly accessed the podium, and therefore the cell, through the main staircase on the front, at the foot of which the faithful stopped, at least judging by the painted representations returned to us from Herculaneum, or, in secret, through the staircase on the S side, hidden behind the protrusion of the left niche.

Cella (3), view from E: the façade is partially covered by the columns of the pronaos (2) but it is possible to recognize the stucco cladding with the smooth plinth and the middle area with two-storey aedicules with hanging crowns, framed laterally by fluted pilasters with tuff capitals originally Corinthian, then covered with stucco in order to transform them into composite capitals. 127. Purgatorium (4): view of the temple of the small uncovered enclosure that protected the staircase leading down to the lustral water basin. On the grooved architrave, interrupted by the door, you can still see the silhouettes of the figurines of offerers, now completely disappeared and documented by eighteenth-century engravings, like the stucco covering of the altar now completely lost.

Purgatorium (4): the enclosure has the appearance of a small temple with the front marked by pilasters that support a grooved architrave, interrupted at the door surmounted by a small arch, inserted in the tympanum of the pediment which retained traces of color. The O-shaped altar is the main altar of the sanctuary (12b) and is moved from the temple so as not to hinder ritual processions. It was found intact, with "the ashes and burnt bones of the victims" on the sacrificial floor which was bordered by a parapet with the corner horns that have now disappeared typical of Ptolemaic altars.

129. Purgatorium (4): the panel of F. The Vega shows the same subjects as in the previous photo but with the altar moved down to allow a complete view of the façade of the enclosure. The mirrors contain a sort of canopy, consisting of a taut carpet from which garlands and an oscillum are hung, under which is an Isiac statue resting on a shelf. The external pilasters contain shoots closed in circles within which there are animals and cult objects, mostly Isiac; the internal ones are crossed by a thin metal candelabrum interrupted by a male figure; the capitals all bear the representation of Harpocrates among acanthus leaves. The figures of the architrave converge in procession towards the door; on the tympanum we can recognize two winged Genii with banners and two kneeling figures on either side of the sacred hydria.

V, p. 550, fig. 138) is treated here, with much more felicitous results: the figures in the stucco relief actually hover in space without the awkwardness of badly crossed feet or unnaturally bent legs as in the fresco.

169. Sacrarium (5), N wall with an arched niche whose walls are made up of reused cipollino pillars. On the left one, in fact, the name of M. Lucretius (Decidianus) Rufus can be read, of which five other similar inscriptions have been found and it is not excluded that the right pillar is also part of the group and that the inscription is on the face against the masonry. In this aedicule was found the statue in blue faience of a crouching male deity, from the Ptolemaic era.

170. Sacrarium (5) wall N: the engraving by N. Billy from the drawing by G. Casanova, presents the wall complete with the painted decoration that was detached in various parts all preserved in the Museum of Naples. The idol of faience in the position of discovery can be recognized in the niche.

171. Sacrarium(5), N wall: in the W corner there was the clumsy image of Bes (MNN, inv. 8916), a rural deity of dance who did not appear in the Egyptian pantheon before the twelfth dynasty and who was represented in all forms of art from the Ptolemaic to the Roman age. Usually on her head she has a rich hairstyle of ostrich feathers that has been replaced here by the lotus flower; he sits on a large stool and has disproportionately frail legs.

172. Sacrarium (5), wall N: to the left of the niche was the most religiously significant painting (MNN, inv. 8929) of any painting in the sanctuary. Between two large busts of river gods, whose iconography recalls the Hellenistic one of Serapis, a moment of the navigium Isidis is represented. The goddess, in a yellow tunic with a white mantle bordered with black and a lotus flower on her head, stands at the stern of a boat of rushes and holds the end of a rope fastened to the human-headed bow of another boat, with lower edges and flatter, on which is a chest that has a falcon painted on one side. It is the transport of sacred water, a reference to Osiris the regenerator, whose body torn apart by the evil Seth, had been recomposed by the goddess and her resurrected love. In the lower register there are two large snakes advancing towards a wicker cist adorned with a crescent moon, and resting on a small pillar that hides the point of origin of two spirals with flowers that are arranged on the sides of it.

173. Sacrarium (5), N wall: the figure of the lion (MNN, inv. 8564) immediately followed towards the E whose tail ended on one of the river personifications. While the rendering of the legs is accurate, the head is now a spot of color with poorly defined details. In front of the right hind leg you can read the traces of another paw, depicted upright, which would have given the feline a standing pose.

174. Sacrarium (5), N wall: the cobra rolled up on itself has a red lotus flower on its head and the threatening attitude, with a swollen neck, typical of the pharaonic iconography that saw in this animal the symbol of Wadjet, the goddess of Lower Egypt. It was probably already in poor condition if it was not re-inventoried after 1826 (MNN, inv. MDXII). Diap. AFSN 36962

175. Sacrarium (5), N wall: at the end of the wall was the white ibis with black neck, legs and wings, with ears of corn in its beak and lotus on its head (MNN, inv. 8562), symbol of Toth, god of wisdom and, in that guise, lunar deity who guides the dead to the afterlife.

176. Sacrarium (5), wall N: it was possible to recognize this almost illegible fragment (MNN, without inv. no., 4) thanks to the comparison of the copper engraving taken for the first time on the occasion of the reopening of the rooms of the Museum of Naples dedicated to the Temple of Isis. The vulture, with its powerful beak and long claws, represented with almost closed wings, was the symbol of Nekhbet, the primordial goddess of Upper Egypt.

177. Sacrarium (5), wall E with the arched door towards the S arm of the portico (1). On this wall was painted the group of animals in the desert and the bull, of which no reproductions remain before the detachment.

178. Sacrarium (5), wall E: the fragment (MNN, inv. 8533) shows on two registers animals typical of the desert areas of Egypt alluded to by the sand dunes and the two slender trees barely hinted at in very diluted colors. The seated baboon, another symbol of Thoth, holding a snake between its paws, can be recognized; followed by a ram, Khnum the god of cataracts; the jackal in an assault position and with his jaws open, symbol of Anubis, the god who had embalmed Osiris, "the one who presides over secrets" and the guardian par excellence. In the upper register we see a mouse, a vulture and a crouching ichneumon, symbol of Horus. It is clear that this depiction had the dual function of evoking the environment of Egypt and accustoming the initiates to the symbolism that was one of the elements characterizing the Isiac ritual and devotion to the goddess.

179. Sacrarium (5), wall E: the bull (MNN, inv. 8565) facing right, with the sun disk between its horns, which in Roman times replaced the crescent moon typical of previous iconography, is an obvious reference to Apis whose ritual funerals took place according to the manner of the cult of Osiris. Under the reddish-brown brushstrokes of the cloak, traces of a band that vertically surrounds the body of the animal can be glimpsed, similar to the one that adorned the bull carried to the sacrifice according to Roman custom, perhaps a mistake by the painter accustomed to other subjects. Diap. AFSN 36958

180. Sacrarium (5), S wall consisting of the external wall of the theatre of which one of the buttresses remains, near which, towards the E, there was a basin raised by a few steps. The articulation of this wall and the eighteenth-century relationships suggest that there were no figurative representations but simply white plaster.

The young woman, recognizable by the horns on her head, is brought from the Nile, with dark flesh like the land of Egypt fertilized by its floods, in the presence of Isis who welcomes her benevolently, accompanied by Harpocrates, who sits next to her, by a priestess and by a priest who, to the properly Isiac symbols of the situla and the sistrum, also associates the sistrum of Hermes,  I therefore probably recall Hermanubis. Isis rests her feet on a crocodile and holds a cobra in her left hand, that is, she dominates the forces of evil, an attitude that is referred to the Isis of Canopus, the place where, according to the Aeschylean tradition, Io finally finds refuge. Next to the personification of the river we see a statue of a sphinx among marsh plants and, in the background of the composition, a large horned altar that characterizes the environment in which the scene takes place as a sanctuary.

The Fox in this ink of 1870 was also notable for the presence of a hexameter of which only a part was read: Barbarus aere cavo tubicen precisely reported in the drawing (cf. Draftsmen, p. 737, fig. 205). Telamon is freeing the young girl from the fetters that chain her to the rock where she had been exposed as prey for the monster that infested Troy, thus punished by Poseidon for Laomedon's deception. Although according to the myth below, it was Heracles who killed the monster lying in the water pierced by an arrow, Telamon intervening in the action, according to the interpretation of the model used by the Pompeian painter, thus deserves the king's daughter in marriage. The particular emphasis given to the drawing of the figure of Telamon, of which the contour line could be seen, has led us to believe (Bd, 1867, p. 84) that the painter carried out a real study of the human figure.
